#744. Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

"We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper.

New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.

NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity.

As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf, the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived "red giant" phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris.

During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space.

To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming.

"Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action."

The team was able to determine that this gas shell of IRAS 06530-0213 is around half a light-year wide and was ejected into space around 6,500 years ago. It represents the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before this kind of star enters the final phase of its life.

The team thinks that for around 2,000 years after the pulse, the star lost mass at a lower rate. This mass loss then increased sharply over the following 1,000 years. This led to the creation of a lumpy shell of gas now seen as a tangle of material filaments around the dying star. The fact that these filaments have a spiral shape could indicate that IRAS 06530-0213 has an unseen partner orbiting it, stirring the gas.

Meanwhile, the hourglass-shaped nebula immediately around the star began to take shape around 700 years ago, meaning that the red giant phase for IRAS 06530-0213 only ended very recently, in cosmic terms at least.

There are also unexpected elements to the ALMA observations of IRAS 06530-0213.

The team discovered an unexpected abundance of heavy versions, or isotopes, of elements like carbon, oxygen and nitrogen around IRAS 06530-0213.

This doesn't conform to models of how stars like IRAS 06530-0213 forge elements and mix them into their surroundings, though similar signatures have been seen around odd stellar objects, with violent bursts of nuclear fusion thought to be the cause.As well as seeing something unexpected, the researchers didn't detect something they expected to observe.

Dying stars like IRAS 06530-0213 have previously been known to have companions, typically sitting with them inside compact disks of dust. These disks are indirect evidence of material being dragged from the close companion star to the dying star. This is a process scientists have used to explain jet-sculpted hourglass shapes.

However, ALMA failed to detect such disk around IRAS 06530. The team suggests that this could be because a disk existed, albeit briefly, during which time it powered a short burst of high-speed jets that helped sculpt the hourglass, following this the disk simply faded away.

"Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres," Sahai concluded. "IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."The team's research was published on Friday (Nov. 20) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Hoda Kotb weighed in after NBC confirmed that the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade would be postponed to Nov. 28: “We waited 100 years for this parade, we’re gonna wait two more days.”

Hoda Kotb knows that sometimes stuffing happens.

After the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed for the first time in its 100-year history, the Joy 101 founder—who was set to host the event alongside Savannah Guthrie and Al Roker—shared why she thinks pushing the event to Nov. 28 was for the best.

“It’s OK,” Kotb said on the November 25 episode of Late Night With Seth Meyers. “We waited 100 years for this parade, we’re gonna wait two more days. We’re gonna have it on Saturday. It’s gonna be a beautiful, sunsplash day.”

As the 62-year-old noted, the date change came about after it was clear the forecast on Thanksgiving Day “was not gonna be fun.”

“The winds were like tropical storm force,” she explained. “There are a bunch of kids who were marching and people with the balloons.”

But Kotb—mom to daughters Haley Joy, 9, and Hope Catherine, 7, with ex Joel Schiffman—is choosing the see the gravy boat half full.

“The good news is, to me, I’m relieved,” the Today alum said. “Saturday’s gonna be amazing. Everybody’s still hanging out. We’re gonna watch it anyway.”

In lieu of the scheduled program, NBC will re-air last year's show at 8 a.m. in all time zones, a spokesperson from the network told E! News in a Nov. 25 statement. And the change in plans won’t rain on Kotb’s parade.

As she put it, “We’re gonna watch an old parade and you won’t know the difference, OK? It’s gonna be spectacular.”

And since the team behind the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has “been working tirelessly for a year-plus” to perfect the event, Kotb teased that it'll be worth the wait.

“The musical acts are incredible,” she said. “It’s gonna be out of this world.”

Kotb’s comments come hours after an NBC spokesperson confirmed to E! News that the beloved event would be postponed due to weather.

“Due to the extreme weather conditions, the city of New York, Macy’s and NBC have decided, in the interest of safety for both the participants and spectators, to move the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday, Nov. 28,” the spokesperson shared in a Nov. 25 statement. “More details to follow.”

And while the postponement marks the first in the parade’s 100-year history, they emphasized that the show will go on.

“Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year,” a spokesperson told MSNOW in a statement. “We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.”

#740. Head coach Slegers leaves Arsenal 18 months after Champions League win

Renee Slegers initially joined Arsenal in 2023 as an assistant coach under Jonas Eidevall

Arsenal have parted company with head coach Renee Slegers by mutual consent after a disappointing start to the season.

Slegers, 37, was initially appointed on an interim basis in October 2024 before being handed the role permanently three months later.

The Dutchwoman led Arsenal to their second Women's Champions League title in May 2025 and the inaugural Fifa Women's Champions Cup in February 2026.

But she leaves with the team sixth in the Women's Super League after 11 matches - 12 points behind leaders Chelsea.

Assistant coach Aaron D'Antino has also left the club, with assistant Melissa Clarke-Reed placed in interim charge as they begin the search for a permanent replacement.

D'Antino had been part of Arsenal's coaching staff since August 2018.

Arsenal director of women's football Clare Wheatley said the decision had been "extremely difficult".

"In leading us to glory in the Champions League and the inaugural Fifa Champions Cup, Renee has made a significant and lasting contribution to the history of Arsenal Football Club, with close support from Aaron," she said.

"After careful reflection, it is clear that results have been below the expected level, and change is necessary."

Chief executive Richard Garlick paid tribute to both departing coaches, describing Slegers as "a wonderful person" who had played "an integral role in some of the most historic achievements in the club's history".

"Our ambition is to compete for and win major trophies consistently, and our recent results have led us to conclude that a change is necessary to give us the best opportunity to achieve those goals," he added.

Why Arsenal are behind in race for Champions League spots

Slegers' departure comes after weeks of pressure as Arsenal's WSL form continued to deteriorate.

While the Dutch coach delivered the Women's Champions League and Women's Champions Cup, results in the league have fallen below expectations this season.

Arsenal have endured a four-match winless run in the league and their struggles have been particularly stark at their own Emirates Stadium, where they have gone six matches without a victory.

For a side expected to challenge for major trophies every season, those dropped points are damaging as they have fallen well adrift of Chelsea and even eight points behind London City Lionesses, who are in the third Women's Champions League qualification spot.

A lack of goals has been central to Arsenal's struggles. They have scored just 11 times in 11 WSL matches this season - less than half the tally of Chelsea (29), second-placed Manchester City (28) and London City Lionesses (31).

Before Slegers' exit was confirmed on Friday, former Arsenal and England forward Lianne Sanderson had called for the manager to depart.

"I've been a big advocate for Renee to stay in the job, but after the Lyon game [a 2-0 home defeat in the Champions League], I felt this feeling in my stomach that it's time [to part ways]," Sanderson told FourFourTwo, external.

"That was probably the most defeated I have felt. The players weren't fighting, they had just shown nothing, there was no identity.

"The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results."

After Sunday's draw with West Ham, Slegers acknowledged performances and results had fallen short of expectations and made it clear she accepted responsibility.

"I love the club," she said. "We're going through a very, very difficult time, and I take my responsibilities, because the results haven't been good enough.

"In the second half we are chasing again, but we're not creating good enough chances to the final third, from all phases, and the way we get there, it's not the Arsenal standard and we need to do that better.

"But I take my responsibilities in my role."

#739. Man Utd trigger Fernandes' one-year contract extension

Bruno Fernandes joined Manchester United in 2020

Manchester United have triggered their one-year option on captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.

The 32-year-old's deal was due to expire next summer but sources say both parties decided it was in their best interests to activate the option through to 2028.

It means overseas clubs will not be able to approach Fernandes when the transfer window opens on 1 January.

The Portugal international confirmed on Tuesday that discussions over a new contract had been paused. Sources say they will resume once United's league position has improved.

Fernandes has made 343 appearances for United, scoring 115 goals, since his Â£47m move from Sporting in January 2020.

Last season he broke the Premier League assists record and scooped all of the individual player of the year awards after an outstanding campaign as United finished third.

While there is doubt over his long-term future, extending the contract means United would be able to command a fee for Fernandes should he leave in the summer.

United had been open to selling Fernandes in the summer of 2025, with Saudi Pro-League club Al Hilal offering a huge deal.

After discussing the situation with his wife, Fernandes decided to stay, though he later said it "hurt" United were willing to sell him. He reiterated on Tuesday he was still ambitious to win the biggest honours in the game.

Fernandes is a doubt for Saturday's Premier League encounter with Brentford after returning from the Champions League trip to Sporting with a virus.

The playmaker, who scored both goals in the 2-2 draw with his former club, but did not train on Friday and head coach Mauricio Pochettino said he would take a decision on his captain's fitness on Saturday morning.

"We are going to assess during the day and then tomorrow see how he is when he wakes up," said Pochettino. "We are not going to take any risks."

Pochettino is preparing for his first home game as Man Utd boss

Pochettino was criticised by former Liverpool and England midfielder Jamie Redknapp on the Overlap earlier this week.

Reference was made to the former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea coach high-fiving Sky Sports reporter Patrick Davidson after his side's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday, as evidence Pochettino had lost his edge.

"When I saw Pochettino at Southampton and I saw him at Tottenham, he looked like he had that Argentinian dog in him," said Redknapp.

"I look at him now and he's high-fiving everyone, he's got the bracelets on, he's got the barnet. I think he's gone too nice."

It seems someone had mentioned the observation to Pochettino as he went off on a tangent at his Friday news conference when asked about a "crazy" first week that included red cards, refereeing errors, disallowed goals and a drone filming training.

"What are we going to do? Start to cry?" he asked. "No. We have to be strong, believe and keep going. I cannot judge the past. Who am I to do that? I was in Cincinnati. I was outside. I need to shut my mouth, say nothing and start from now.

"Sometimes we are so confusing two words that means something similar; nice and good. I am not nice. We have to be good. It is a different thing. We know when we need to push, when we need to be strong, and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything.

Pochettino also confirmed Â£70m midfielder Carlos Baleba is expected to be out until the last week in January with the hamstring injury he sustained against Roma on 3 November.

Forward Marcus Rashford had begun to do individual work outside as he tries to recover from a hip problem that has kept him out since 13 October.

'Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner.''

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

#736. Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.

He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#731. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#728. Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair

Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.

Since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

#727. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

#724. Why the incoming US Congress should ban the development of self-improving AI

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alex Bores is a US politician in the New York State Assembly in New York City, New York, USA, and a co-founder of AI-safety advocacy group Who Decides.

The recent US midterm elections were a democratic test of the country’s rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Data centres emerged as a key issue in several election campaigns, and prominent Democrats have outlined policies to strengthen federal regulations on AI once they take office in January.

I am a Democratic politician trained in computer science who stood in a June congressional primary election that attracted millions of dollars from groups backed by the technology industry (I narrowly lost my race). I took one central message from the midterm election results: US voters are unhappy with the industry-led roll-out of AI and want greater control over how the technology is developed and deployed.

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

The newly elected US Congress must respond to the popular mood. An immediate priority should be to ban AI systems that can improve themselves without human authorization or oversight. This process, known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), is thought to be close to realization at some frontier AI laboratories. Voters fear that granting such autonomy to the technology would risk surrendering human control over AI altogether.

Most of the major AI companies are already using the technology to automate parts of AI development. Anthropic reported in August that its Claude model assists with more than 90% of the firm’s AI research and development and leads 26% of that work, completing specific tasks under human supervision. OpenAI, meanwhile, notes that its researchers now use more than three days of AI-agent work for every day of human work. And the firm is open about its eventual goal of full automation, including areas in which AI systems could design and build increasingly powerful successors with little or no human oversight.

In my view, this is a dangerous path, particularly because there is enough evidence on what could go wrong when humans lose control of AI agents. In July, some 700 OpenAI agents unexpectedly coordinated to hack into the servers of Hugging Face, another AI firm. In a separate incident in October, AI agents found ways to manipulate the records of their actions, making their behaviour harder for humans to monitor. If AI systems increasingly participate in building their successors, such failures could intensify. (OpenAI has not responded to requests for comment.)

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

The companies are racing each other to market dominance, and against that economic pull, no voluntary norm will stand. Hence, Congress must step in. A ban on fully autonomous RSI would build on a rare area of cross-partisan agreement: individuals from independent senator Bernie Sanders to Republican political strategist Steve Bannon think that humans must remain in control of AI.

To be effective, such a ban must be specific. A person merely clicking ‘approve’ on thousands of AI-proposed experiments each day is not exercising meaningful control. The law should instead prevent AI systems from independently taking consequential steps in AI development, such as launching a training run for a new frontier model or deploying it internally for AI research. One way to do this would be to require a senior executive to certify that qualified human reviewers have examined the proposed changes and relevant safety evaluations before any development actions proceed. Executives should be personally liable for failing to perform oversight duties.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03849-8

A.B. is co-founder of Who Decides, an advocacy group that seeks to shape the policy discussions around AI for the 2028 Democratic presidential field. It will do so by working with local organizations across the early primary and swing states — it will not endorse or spend for specific candidates.

#723. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

#721. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.

November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.

Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.

Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in New York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.

Hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of New York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon snapped a series of stunning photos from the International Space Station on Nov. 24, November full moon slipped out of view below Earth's horizon, while being gradually deformed by the warping effect of our planet's atmosphere. "Moonset today from space station - no edits to these photos from 400mm lens," Menon wrote in a post on X.

Heading back down to Earth Salih Zeki Fazlioglu took a colorful photo of the Beaver moon illuminating a thin veil of clouds above Istanbul, Turkiye, as reflected sunlight competed with the artificial glow of the city below for the viewer's attention.

This shot of the lunar disk looming over the Old Post Office Pavillion in Washington D.C. was captured by David Ake, with the pink sky complementing the orange and red leaves of autumn.

Our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.

"Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up."

This striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.

Allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.

"Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image."

Moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?

Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.

That Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.

Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

Feeling inspired to capture your own supermoon photos? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the moon and browse our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography because you don't have long to wait!

The final supermoon of 2026 rises in just a few short weeks on Dec. 23 and it just so happens to be the closest full moon of the year, passing just 221,668 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth at the point of maximum illumination.

So no excuses! We'd love to see your photo in our inbox next month.

#719. Sean “Diddy” Combs’ Prison Thanksgiving Meal Revealed

Sean “Diddy” Combs is spending his third Thanksgiving behind bars this year, and his Turkey Day meal is set to include all the fixings.

Sean “Diddy” Combs isn’t skipping out on Turkey Day.

After all, the rapper—who is serving a 50-month prison sentence for prostitution related charges at FCI Allenwood Low in Pennsylvania—will enjoy a full-course meal come Nov. 26, a law enforcement official at the prison confirmed to People.

Combs' Thanksgiving menu includes a choice between turkey and tofu stir-fry, they told the outlet, along with sides like mashed potatoes and candied sweet potato casserole.

And it appears the music mogul will be able to enjoy all the fixings as the menu also features green bean casserole, sage and onion stuffing and dinner rolls, the official confirmed. Combs will also have his choice of gravy and cranberry sauce for the meal.

And what’s Thanksgiving without dessert? This year, the 57-year-old will satisfy his sweet tooth with pecan pie.

E! News has reached out to Combs’ rep for comment but did not hear back.

But not every inmate will be getting the same spread. In fact, the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) does not offer a standardized holiday menu across all facilities. Rather, some have more flexibility with their menus than others.

Holiday meals “reflect available food items, local considerations, and the cultural diversity of the inmate population,” a spokesperson told Oxygen. “This allows institutions to incorporate menu enhancements and provide meals that recognize the specific holiday.”

The statement added, “The same goes for any planned activities at each facility.”

Though this Thanksgiving marks Combs’ third behind bars, it’s his first at FCI Allenwood Low, where he was transferred in October after sustaining a head injury while incarcerated at New Jersey's FCI Fort Dix.

"His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction, and while we cannot speak to the BOP's specific reasons for the move, it is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind,” Combs’ rep told E! in an Oct. 16 statement. "We are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption."
