#626. Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal important details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory

Researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

The researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover new details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Big Bang.

"Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," says Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside."

Du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery

The origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion."

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

He demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

In conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

"Einstein showed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did."

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

The team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

They then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

At first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

"The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis says. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected."

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

Even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

"This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis says. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks."

The discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Big Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

The results also point toward an important characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

Du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas."

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising new approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

The research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.

#625. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars.

The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars, or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past.

It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a new landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface.

It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet.

Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success.

After its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars. It later found organic molecules on Mars as well.

Curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health.

In fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover, which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars.

And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise, is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon.

#623. Candace Cameron Bure Says She Gets “Substantial” Residuals From ‘Full House’

The actress played D.J. Tanner throughout the show's run from 1987 to 1995, and later reprised her role in the sitcom’s spin-off 'Fuller House.'

Candace Cameron Bure is getting candid about the residuals she still earns from Full House.

The actress appeared on a recent episode of The McBride Rewind podcast, where she revealed that she gets “substantial” payouts from the sitcom, which ran for eight seasons from 1987 to 1995.

“They’re substantial… I think it’s like quarterly,” she said, noting that while some residual checks for other projects might be a few cents or dollars, the ones for Full House are “still substantial.” Related Stories Lifestyle Dave Coulier Says Cancer Treatment Has Led to Changes in His Speech and Physical Appearance Movies Why Candace Cameron Bure Says Horror Films Can Lead to a "Portal" That's "Incredibly Demonic"

“I’m always happy when I open that check and deposit it,” Bure added.

The actress played D.J. Tanner, the eldest sister to Stephanie (Jodie Sweetin) and Michelle (Mary-Kate/Ashley Olsen), throughout the show’s run. She also reprised her role in the sitcom’s spin-off Fuller House, which ran for five seasons from 2016 to 2020.

Host Josh McBride also brought up Sweetin’s appearance on the podcast in April 2026, where she shared that her residuals aren’t as great as they used to be.

“I got a one-cent check the other day. No, there’s no syndication anymore because it’s all in streaming. Who gets paid for that? Nobody gets paid for that,” Sweetin said at the time. “Sure, in my 20s, there would be money, but not reliable. You don’t know how much it’s going to be or how often they’re going to run the show. So, sometimes you’re like, ‘Oh, cool. That was nice.’ And then sometimes you’re like, ‘All right, well, there’s a nice dinner out.'”

In response, Bure told McBride, “I actually saw that and she said she doesn’t get much now. And I was like, ‘Jodie, you gotta check with your agent or you gotta call your bank,’ ’cause I still get residuals.”

Elsewhere on the podcast, Bure also addressed the Olsen twins’ decision not to appear on the spin-off. “It was a bummer because it would have been fun to have everybody back,” she said of Fuller House. “But at the same time, it wasn’t surprising just because none of us really have stayed close with the girls.”

“Not because anything went wrong or there was any bad blood. I just think they were kids. They were [filming from] 9 months old until they were 8 years old. They have very different memories than we do. Even me being 10 years older than them, I have significant, great, wonderful memories,” she continued. “They were babies. They probably don’t even remember half the stuff [we do]. They didn’t have the attachment to the crew and the people like we did being older. And they had such a successful fashion business. They haven’t been actors for a long time. They just haven’t been in that part of entertainment.”

#622. FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?

Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?

Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.

Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.

During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.

At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.

Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.

A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.

Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.

He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).

"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.

"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."

Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.

The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.

During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.

"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.

"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."

Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.

But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.

"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he said.

"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.

However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.

If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

#621. DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage

The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," said Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule."

This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

New Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team plan to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins."

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

#619. Justin Timberlake Rolls Back the Years on Silly, Sexy and Sincere Appearance on ‘Tonight Show’

The singer performed a medley of his hits, took part in some dumb sketches and bared his soul about why he agreed to take part in an upcoming Apple TV docuseries.

A game Justin Timberlake gave a welcome reminder of his varied talents on The Tonight Show on Thursday night, variously dressing up as a “sexy” turkey, doing a spirited Scottish accent and of course dancing and singing like only he can.

In what felt like a throwback to the innocence and goofiness of the Obama years, Timberlake was on top form, taking part in sketches, dance bits and sitting down for an interview to promote the 20th anniversary of his classic album FutureSex/LoveSounds and the four-part documentary series Timberlake that begins streaming on Apple TV on Dec. 11. Related Stories TV Justin Timberlake Documentary Trailer: "He's Not Who I Thought He Was" Music Justin Timberlake Teases New Music: "I've Been Chef-ing"

With the Roots backing them up, Fallon opened the show with Timberlake for a song and dance number, with the duo going through The History of Party Songs. In a segment that is catnip for 90s kids, the tracks covered included Soul II Soul’s “Back to Life (However Do You Want Me),” Ini Kamoze’s “Here Comes the Hotstepper,” Mark Morrison’s “Return of the Mack,” Montell Jordan’s “This Is How We Do It,” Spice Girls “Wannabe,” Bell Biv DeVoe’s “Poison,” Timberlake’s own “Rock Your Body” and more.

In the interview section, Timberlake opened up about the making of FutureSex/LoveSounds, reminding the audience that that his influences on the album included “Bowie, David Byrne, Talking Heads, Freddie Mercury, Queen, Billy Idol, James Brown, Eurythmics and INXS.” He said that on the song “SexyBack” he was channeling Bowie doing “Rebel Rebel” and he had to fight the recording company on the production. “They fought me on it. Well, I brought it in and it was like, ‘It’s too fast.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.’ … [And they said], ‘You don’t sound like you, your signature falsetto.’ I was like, ‘That’s why it’s gonna work.'”

On the infamous lyrics to “SexyBack”, Timberlake added, “That song does not make any sense. I’ve said this. It makes zero sense. But, it’s why it makes sense.”

In a particularly poignant part of the interview, Timberlake discussed his love for and influence of the late D’Angelo, describing him as “my guy.” “D’Angelo, for me, he changed everything. You know, he was one of those artists… rest in peace. What a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant artist. But I remember when he came out, it just like everything changed. [He] was a once-in-a-generation artist.”

On why he decided to take part in the Apple docuseries — which Fallon said tackled Timberlake’s career highpoints and personal low points — the Grammy-winner said that initially he “was really reluctant to do it” agreeing with Fallon that he was “sort of famously private.” His relationship with director Fisher Stevens softened his stance and that the doc he has “mustered up some courage to talk about some things that I’ve never talked about before, that, you know, things that even those that are closest to me don’t know.”

Timberlake said he found the doc experience “cathartic” and he hoped it would help others to share their troubles. “Everybody’s going through something. And I think I’ve gone through a lot in the last five years that I feel like have made me a better human and a better father, a better husband, a better friend.”

In the recent past, Timberlake has had a number of public incidents including being arrested for DWI in the Hamptons in June 2024 and revealing in July 2025 that he was diagnosed with Lyme disease. There was also the cheating rumors in 2019, and subsequent public ridicule, after the singer was caught holding hands with co-star Alisha Wainwright during the filming of Palmer. Timberlake had to issue a public apology about the Palmer incident on Instagram, calling it a “strong lapse in judgment.”

One sketch that’s likely to get a lot of play on social media was “Sexy Butterball Hotline,” where Fallon (Rocky Drumstick) and Timberlake (Pecker Spatchcock) played two very sexy turkeys — “the dirtiest birds in the coop” no less — manning an after dark Thanksgiving helpline. A sample of some of the lines from Rocky and Pecker in this bit: “Who says the turkey can’t be the one who does the stuffing?” “Is it Black Friday? ‘Cause my clothes are 100% off.” “I can’t wait till you lay me down on the table right in front of Grandma.” Good clean fun.

It wouldn’t be a complete Timberlake Tonight Show appearance without a “Camp Winnipesaukee” sketch. Fallon and Timberlake once more donned the retainers and wigs to relive their awkward teenage years and play the annoying campers trying to sing a popular song much to the annoyance of the camp counselor. On Thursday’s episode, the pair decided to take on The Proclaimers’ 1988 hit “I’m Gonna Be (500 Miles)” with Timberlake and Fallon’s attempt at Scottish brogue worthy of commendation but ultimately short of passable.

Proving he’s still one of the greatest singers and dancers around, Timberlake rounded his appearance with two medleys of his greatest hits. In the first clip he performed a medley of “FutureSex / LoveSound,” “SexyBack,” “Summer Love” and “My Love.”

In a second clip he performed “LoveStoned,” “Until the End of Time” and “What Goes Around…/ … Comes Around.”

#618. Arthur Conti Was Booked This Year With Roles in ‘Carrie’ and ‘Ebenezer.’ Now He’s Looking to Get “a Little Strange”

The 22-year-old has tackled iconic characters in pop culture this year, but he's keeping himself open about what's next.

British actor Arthur Conti is fresh off a whirlwind year. With roles in Mike Flanagan’s Carrie adaptation and the recently released Ebenezer, he’s been busy crafting new interpretations of well-known characters.

“To play an iconic character that’s been played by many people before, and to get to give your own spin on it, is very exciting,” Conti tells The Hollywood Reporter over Zoom from London about what he’s been up to this year.

The 22-year-old actor is back in the U.K. after over a month of press for Carrie and Ebenezer and a stint in Portland, Oregon. “It’s been a bit of a whirlwind, but it’s been very enjoyable,” he says. After a breakout performance in 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, 2026 has been the actor’s biggest year to date between the two projects and a role in Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Related Stories TV Why Mike Flanagan Just Couldn't Kill Carrie White Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Slays $120M at Box Office as Franchise Heats Back Up

With Carrie, Conti stepped into the role of teen bully Billy Nolan, first played on screen by John Travolta in Brian De Palma’s 1976 film. Conti had read Stephen King’s novel but hadn’t seen De Palma’s film, which he stayed away from during filming. Conti’s Billy, while still one of the villains of the story, is different from Travolta’s take on the character. “I was worried that even inadvertently or subconsciously I would copy things about that performance, and I really wanted it to be all my own,” he says.

Ebenezer finds Conti stepping into the shoes of the titular character of Ebenezer Scrooge — well, the younger version of him anyway. The actor heard that Ti West would be making the film, and as a big fan, he sent in a self-tape. Much like with Carrie, he tried not to take too much inspiration from previous versions of the story, but there’s one adaptation that stands out.

“[The Muppets version] is probably the best one. I mean, it’s amazing, that film. Michael Caine gives such a genuinely brilliant, dramatic performance in that film against the Muppets,” he says. “He takes it so seriously, and that is the beauty of that film is that you’d think he was talking to John Gielgud, and he’s talking to Fozzy.”

Despite The Muppets Christmas Carol being his main experience with the story beforehand, he did watch the 1951 film adaptation starring Alastair Sim as Scrooge. “I really liked,” he notes.

Below, the actor digs into his last year in roles, what he’s looking to do next and how he’d spend a perfect day in London.

I’m always curious, as someone who enjoys it — have you seen Carrie: The Musical?

We watched it. We saw a theater production on Granville Island in Vancouver. It was a youth theater production of Carrie: The Musical. [The cast of Carrie] all went to go and see it. Mike [Flanagan] actually put the cast of that production of Carrie in the show. They’re all at the prom. Throughout the show, they’re in the background at the school, which was really, really fun.

How has the year been? You were busy with Carrie and now Ebenezer.

[Carrie] was my first big press tour. It was my first time doing a press junket and all of these things. It feels like the biggest thing that I’ve done so far [with] how much I’ve been promoting it. It was all incredibly exciting. [In Carrie,] I’m playing another character that has several sides to him, after [I did in] Beetlejuice. It’s another deceptively charming, manipulative character, which is interesting that I keep taking. (Laughs).

Something about me, I don’t know. Something untrustworthy. Honestly, it is a treat to play characters like that because you get the chance to do multiple things at once, present a character that has many layers and is complex and isn’t wholly one thing or another. It was a great role. It was a really meaty role to sink my teeth into, and it was an honor to play a character of that literary significance. It was a privilege to be entrusted with that.

As an actor, are you drawn to characters that are different from you, then?

It’s nice to get outside of yourself — that’s part of the fun of it. Growing up, the films I was watching, I was a lot more drawn to flawed or strange or darker characters. I grew up watching Steve Buchemi in Fargo and Philip Seymour Hoffman in Punch-Drunk Love and Talented Mr. Ripley. Those are the kind of characters that I always really loved to watch.

The scope of the projects you had this year has been quite large. Are you drawn to that or looking to change it?

You’re right. They are quite large-scale. I think I’m drawn to things that are a little out there and a little strange. Horror is one of the best genres to explore that area because it emboldens filmmakers to experiment and take risks and be a bit weird and a bit dreamlike. That’s why I gravitate towards horror a lot, and it’s probably what I watch the most of in the cinema.

Is that where you got your love for it? Were you big into horror as a kid?

I think so. It’s not horror, just things that are a little strange. My mom brought me up on Charlie Kaufman films. Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is my mom’s favorite film, so I watched that quite early. Things that tap into that dreaminess and that weirdness and spookiness — that’s up my alley. But it would be a dream to do a Before Sunrise kind of thing, where it’s just two people talking for an hour and a half. I would love to do something like that next.

Is that what you’re looking to do going forward then?

It could be anything. I really want to leave myself open. I would love to do something a little more scaled down, kind of dialogue-heavy thing. I could never have imagined the caliber of director and the caliber of actor that I’ve been working with. If I can only just continue to do that, I will be very lucky indeed. I’ve gotten to work with some of my absolute heroes, and that’s been wonderful. But I want to keep working in horror as well. Horror’s having a really exciting moment right now, especially young people in horror, with Obsession and Backrooms. I will stay as long as it’ll have me. Horror, fantasy — that’s what I grew up with, and I want to explore that more as well.

I would wake up at 10:30 a.m.-ish. I’m a very late-to-bed, late-to-rise kind of person in my free time. I’d wake up then; I’d get a coffee; I’d go for a walk. I have to do 10,000 steps a day. I’m like a dog. I have to be walked. Then I would go and see a movie. I would go to the cinema. I would probably go to the Prince Charles Cinema, which is my favorite in the world. I don’t know whether I’d see it on my own or with somebody else. I do go on my own to the cinema a lot. That’s one of my favorite ways to watch a film. Then I’d get a nice dinner. I might go shopping a little bit. I might go record shopping, go DVD shopping. Then I would go to the pub maybe, and then I would go to bed at 1 a.m. I’m being very specific with the times.

I’m unfamiliar with Prince Charles Cinema; why is that your favorite theater?

Just the vibe there, and the programming. There’s always something on there that’s worth seeing. I honestly have so much to thank that cinema for because the education in film that it has given me is just insane. I’ve seen so many films there for the first time. It’s one of the few places, in London especially, where you can see old films and cult films and things that don’t get screened very often. You can go and experience them in the theater, and that’s a very valuable thing. They were going to possibly get shut down, but they’ve just won the battle against the landlord or whatever. They’re going to be there for another 25 years. I’m very happy about that.

#617. Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV

In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.

Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.

A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.

The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing."

The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.

According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.

It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.

Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.

In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.

Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.

Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.

Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once."

Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.

"These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth."

This article has been translated from German.

Venus reaches peak brightness in the predawn sky this week, here's how to find it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know.

As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.

Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane.

Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky. Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below.

This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification.

The bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky.

Spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope.

Check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease.

Want to get a closer look at the planets of the solar system and the stars beyond? Then be sure to check out our roundups of the best telescopes and smart telescopes for observing the night sky.

#615. A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve important biological functions.

In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

This research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject."

Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine."

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island

Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#614. The Ultimate Thanksgiving Detox? Mexico’s Most Over-the-Top, Celeb-Approved Longevity Clinic

A new wellness resort is attracting a glittery crowd with outré longevity offerings. Rectal ozone therapy, anyone?

Pampering spa getaways are so passé. The reinvented power trip? Longevity-centered five-star resorts that zero in on preventive medicine and rigorous cutting-edge health-optimization treatments. Think Benjamin Button-like cellular reprogramming and biotech breakthroughs that promise to help rewind biological aging in the elite quest to amp up health span.

Once confined largely to Switzerland, top-tier medi-wellness destinations are moving closer to Hollywood. Most notable among them is SHA Mexico, which opened in 2024 on a beachfront stretch of Costa Mujeres, north of Cancún. The flagship avant-garde longevity clinic, SHA Spain, launched in 2008 in the coastal town of L’Albir, has welcomed pro athletes, royalty, supermodels and such stars as Barbra Streisand (for repeat visits), Demi Moore, Monica Bellucci, Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz, Lily James, Madonna and Marisa Tomei. Now names like Dakota Johnson, Kate Moss, Jack Black, Pink, model Candice Swanepoel and Lake Bell are on the guest list at the Mexican outpost. Related Stories Lifestyle The 5 Best Red Light Therapy Panels for Improving Your Health At-Home Lifestyle Jennifer Aniston Joins Boyfriend Jim Curtis For Chat About Health, Wellness and Hypnotherapy

Calling to mind The Jetsons’ Googie-style home in Orbit City, the futuristic design, by Mexican architecture studio Sordo Madaleno, was aptly inspired by the human genome. Exclusive to this location is a bank of stem cells, unveiled in June, ethically sourced from embryonic tissues for medical and aesthetic cellular regeneration therapies that target autoimmune disease, muscle injuries, sleep apnea, aging skin and more. (At SHA Spain, therapies use the patient’s own stem cells; these donor-derived regenerative treatments are not yet approved in the U.S. or Europe for the uses described.) Treatments are administered through intravenous infusions, nebulizer inhalation and targeted injection; exosome facials inject the cell-derived donor particles directly into the face.

“These therapies reprogram the body’s natural mechanisms to heal and rejuvenate from the inside out,” says Dr. Andrea Márquez, head of SHA’s regenerative medicine, explaining that aging or inflamed cellular systems need a reboot.

A Cell Regeneration Therapy bed with a “human regenerator device” is said to boost energy, support physical recovery and promote anti-aging benefits by surrounding the body with a field of electrically charged particles.

A popular European beauty secret, not yet available in the U.S. and offered at SHA Mexico, is Profhilo, the Italian hyaluronic acid-based skin remodeling injectable that improves elasticity.

More than 200 SHA offerings range from neurocognitive, hormonal and sleep health to genomic medicine, dermatology and physiotherapy. Each guest is prescribed teas and an anti-inflammatory vegan or pescatarian diet, with add-ons like seaweed or shots of apple cider vinegar. SHA’s Japanese-influenced dietary rules discourage liquid drinks during meals (said to “hinder digestion”), and breakfast kicks off with a bowl of miso soup (probiotic-rich to support gut health).

One gut-health package popular with the Hollywood crowd promises to detox and optimize the digestive system. Included are an intestinal dysbiosis analysis, visceral osteopathy (hands-on manipulation of the abdomen intended to improve function of internal organs) and intestinal ozone therapy. Not FDA-approved as a medical treatment in the U.S., the latter pumps an oxygen/ozone gas mixture into the rectum to purportedly “reduce oxidative stress, support immune balance and promote tissue repair,” according to the SHA website.

Gwyneth Paltrow and self-proclaimed “father of biohacking” Dave Asprey have both fessed to using rectal ozone therapy. Vaginal ozone therapy and ozone IV infusions (also used by Asprey) are additionally on the service menu, as is a dental cleaning that incorporates the agent.

Hollywood dermatologist Ava Shamban (whose clients include Moore, Angela Bassett, Nicole Kidman and Michelle Yeoh) weighs in on donor stem cells and ozone treatments: “I say proceed with caution. The science is soft. The good news is that we are on the cusp of truly groundbreaking longevity sciences that will come with DNA optimization and literal reversal of aging, using the newest technologies.”

As over-the-top as some of this may seem, SHA’s owners are firmly at the forefront of longevity research: “It’s not just about trendy biohacking and optimization; we have built a legacy approaching longevity through the lens of both Western functional medicine and Eastern holistic practices,” says SHA managing partner Alejandro Bataller, whose father, Alfredo Bataller, was inspired to found the company after integrative medicine and nutritional shifts helped him overcome early stage colon cancer.

All-inclusive rooms at SHA Mexico run $600 to $9,000 a night, plus program rates starting at $4,800 for a four-night stay. In late June, SHA’s umbrella company, AB Living Group, opened St. Regis Costa Mujeres Resort & Residences next door with a luxe spa, 24-hour butler service, daily champagne sabrage and guest access to SHA. For those who want to truly live the lifestyle, private SHA Residences start at $2.5 million. Next up is SHA Emirates (billed as “the world’s first longevity island”), slated to open in AlJurf, along the coast between Dubai and Abu Dhabi, in early 2028. Residences there will cost $27 million.

#613. Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

Ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide important clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

New research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Important Clues

Dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

"The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan said.

"Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth."

"By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment."

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts

To investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

These findings offer a new perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

The implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth

"The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan said.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a new era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side."

The return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

#612. Denis Villeneuve “Deeply Disappointed” Disney Put ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Against ‘Dune 3’

The director breaks silence on going head-to-head against Marvel's titan on "Dunesday."

Everybody has found it pretty cute, if slightly baffling, that expected box-office heavyweights Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday are opening on the same day (Dec. 18).

But Dune franchise director Denis Villeneuve isn’t amused by going head-to-head with the Marvel titan.

Villeneuve explains in a new interview that he was “deeply disappointed” by the “Dunesday” scheduling, but that Warner Bros. was basically trapped in the slot because the studio had successfully secured an exclusive run on IMAX screens for Dune 3 through the December holidays. Related Stories Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Eyes $270M Opening as 'Dune: Part Three' Also Heads for Big Start Movies 'Avengers: Doomsday' Final Trailer Shows Major X-Men Moment

“Listen, I will be honest,” he told Time. “The first Dune came out at the end of the pandemic. We made a great box office in a very rough environment. But we had the winds against us. Then the second movie, same thing. We were meant to release in the fall, and we had to release at the end of winter because of the two Hollywood strikes. We had success, but it was not easy. The third time, I said to myself, ‘Finally, there is no pandemic, no strike in sight. We will have a normal release.’ Then Disney put the biggest franchise of all time against us. I’m no fool. Those movies are a mammoth.”

“So I was deeply disappointed,” continued the director. “But we had committed to this date, to IMAX. It was impossible to move. So I accepted my fate, praying to the gods of cinema. Dune is not a mammoth like the Avengers, but it’s a sexy little animal that has a lot of firepower, and I hope we will survive. It could be one of the biggest box-office weekends of all time because of both movies. Am I in competition with the Avengers? Absolutely not. It’s a T. rex. But I stand proud because I think the film delivers.”

Both films have notably broken presales records. Dune: Part Three has reportedly bested Warner Bros. all-time presales record, selling more than $30 million worth of tickets for IMAX screens alone (the studio hasn’t released its own all-theater presales numbers). But Doomsday has recently surpassed $100 million and has received the highest initial opening-weekend forecast in NRG tracking history ($270 million). So there’s no world in which both films aren’t big hits, but also no world in which Doomsday doesn’t clock Dune on opening weekend.

Villeneuve also defended making some significant changes to Dune saga author Frank Herbert’s source material for the third film, particularly in the storyline of Chani (Zendaya). “When you adapt, you kill,” he said. “It is not the book. It is my movie inspired by the book, with tremendous respect … I had the idea to make Chani more of a critic regarding the idea of religious colonization … In the third movie, Chani is still a critic of the choices Paul has made. She believes the Fremen should free themselves. She doesn’t want to harm Paul, but she does want to harm his regime. I would have loved to have taken Frank Herbert for a coffee about these ideas because I think he could have liked them. In the book, Chani is there to give Paul foot massages. It’s a character that has not a lot of firepower.”
