#591. Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation

Astronomers have identified an extraordinary pair of quasars dating back to just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Each is powered by an enormous black hole that somehow grew to an astonishing size when the Universe was still in its infancy. Scientists have no definitive explanation for how these two cosmic giants became so massive so quickly. The remarkable pair has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua.

An international research team has discovered the most distant compact pair of quasars ever observed, offering a rare glimpse into the earliest stages of cosmic history. Officially designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the early period known as cosmic dawn.

Although astronomers believe paired quasars should be relatively common, finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult. Discovering two so close together, especially from such an early period in the Universe's history, makes this finding particularly remarkable.

The discovery was made possible by combining observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawai'i. The research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Gemini North is one of the two telescopes that make up the International Gemini Observatory. Operated by NSF NOIRLab, the observatory is an international partnership led by the U.S. National Science Foundation, with participation from Canada, Chile, Brazil, Argentina, and the Republic of Korea.

How Giant Black Holes Formed in the Early Universe

During the first billion years after the Big Bang, the Universe underwent a period of extraordinary transformation. Vast concentrations of invisible matter, known as dark matter halos, collapsed under gravity. The earliest galaxies began producing stars, while increasingly massive galaxies developed the first supermassive black holes at their centers.

As galaxies passed near one another, collided, and sometimes merged, enormous quantities of gas and stars became available to feed their central black holes. Some of the material falling toward these black holes released tremendous amounts of energy. This process, known as accretion, could generate radiation so intense that the glowing region surrounding a black hole outshone every star in its host galaxy.

Astronomers call these extraordinarily luminous objects quasars.

Because galaxy encounters and mergers occur frequently throughout the Universe, researchers expect many quasars to exist in pairs separated by distances smaller than the typical diameter of a galaxy. Yet detecting these systems has remained a major challenge.

One reason is that a supermassive black hole spends only a relatively brief period in its bright "quasar phase." Another is the enormous distance separating ancient quasars from Earth, which makes them appear extremely faint to ground-based telescopes. Even when both objects are visible, their close proximity can make it difficult to distinguish one from the other.

Two Monster Black Holes That Grew Too Big, Too Fast

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua stands out because it is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn. More importantly, its two black holes were already so enormous at such an early stage of cosmic history that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth.

The black holes are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, equivalent to about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. One has an estimated mass of 1.5 billion Suns, while the other weighs approximately 400 million solar masses.

Astronomers see the pair as it appeared only 900 million years after the Big Bang, when the Universe was still populated by relatively young stars, galaxies, and black holes. Finding two black holes comparable in mass to many present-day supermassive black holes at this early time raises difficult questions about how quickly the first enormous cosmic structures could assemble.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two," says Onorato. "We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

The pair's Hawaiian name reflects the extraordinary forces involved. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua translates to "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe."

The name was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai'i's Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).[1]

How James Webb and Gemini North Revealed the Hidden Pair

The discovery began with data collected by the Aether survey, a JWST research program designed to identify and characterize objects from the early Universe. The project is led by Emanuele Paolo Farina, an Associate Scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini.

Using JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit, the survey assembled observations of 200 quasars. That sample represents approximately 43% of all quasars known from this period of cosmic history.

While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed something unexpected. A previously identified quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion.

To investigate, the team turned to Gemini North's Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS). These observations allowed astronomers to distinguish the two quasars individually, providing crucial evidence about the nature of the system.

Obtaining those measurements was an exceptional achievement. The objects are separated by such a small apparent distance, and the companion J1602+4228B is so faint, that resolving them with a telescope on Earth was expected to be nearly impossible.

Fortunately, the researchers benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea. Clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions enabled them to gather the necessary observations in just two nights.

"The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights," says Onorato.

The team also used Gemini North's Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional information about the system and refine their understanding of the two quasars.[2]

A New Clue to the Universe's First Giant Galaxies

Exactly how Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua formed remains unknown. However, the researchers believe its extraordinary properties could point to an unusually dense concentration of matter in the early Universe.

In such an environment, frequent interactions between young galaxies may have provided enormous supplies of gas, simultaneously accelerating the birth of stars and fueling rapid growth of the black holes at their centers.

If this interpretation is correct, the quasar pair could help scientists understand how the earliest massive galaxies developed alongside their central supermassive black holes.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," says Onorato. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

#590. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

Training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates.

Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding.

In the snapshot, the crew — from left to right, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick (mission commander) and Frank Rubio (mission specialist), European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano (mission pilot) and NASA astronaut Andre Douglas (mission specialist) — is spotted posing alongside the same Orion spacecraft that they will fly to space as part of their mission.

This brief moment of levity took place where the spacecraft currently resides at the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

This crew has a serious mission ahead of them. The four astronauts will launch to low-Earth orbit around Earth where they plan to practice rendezvous and docking with both Blue Origin and SpaceX's lunar landing vehicles, Blue Moon and Starship, respectively.

To prepare, the crew has to undergo months of critical training to both be physically ready while prepared to handle any situation that might come up during their mission. And while Artemis III isn't landing astronauts on the moon, it is a critical step toward that goal. If Artemis III goes to plan and NASA has a lunar landing vehicle that passes rendezvous and docking tests with the Orion spacecraft, Artemis IV might see astronauts land on the moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

#588. ‘GTA 6′ Developer Rockstar Games’ Workers Vote Against Union Recognition (Gaming News Roundup)

Employees of “Grand Theft Auto VI” developer Rockstar Games voted against union recognition this week.

In a Nov. 26 vote that included 1,544 staff members (93.2% voter turnout across the Rockstar Games workforce), 75.3% voted against Rockstar Game Workers Union’s recognition with the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) and 24.7% voted in support.

As a result of the vote, Rockstar Games is not required to recognize the union and regularly engage in collective bargaining with reps. #587. This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

A tiny California spider named after comedian Stephen Colbert is making a big impression on scientists. Although it is only about the size of a quarter, the spider has a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.

The species, known as Aptostichus stephencolberti, is a trapdoor spider that lives in California's coastal dunes. Its unusually large genome seems particularly fitting given Colbert's famously pompous television persona on the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report."

Many spiders reach their largest size in the fall after spending the summer feeding, making them familiar symbols of Halloween. But this particular spider stands out for something that cannot be seen with the naked eye: the extraordinary amount of DNA packed into its tiny body.

"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," said corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology.

According to Bond, this is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider belonging to this family. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity.

A Secretive Spider That Hunts From Underground

Visitors to the coastal dunes of Northern California may unknowingly pass close to these spiders without ever spotting one. Most of their lives unfold beneath the sand, where they remain hidden in carefully constructed burrows.

Female trapdoor spiders spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged entrance that blends into its surroundings, allowing the spider to stay concealed while monitoring activity outside.

When an unsuspecting insect or other prey animal approaches, vibrations alert the spider to its presence. At precisely the right moment, the spider bursts through its hidden door to capture its next meal.

Although these spiders are skilled ambush predators, their venom poses no danger to humans. Bond noted that among the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people.

A Spider Genome Bigger Than the Human Genome

The spider's DNA contains more surprises than its sheer size. Researchers found that its genome includes 52 chromosomes, compared with the 46 chromosomes typically found in human cells, which are organized into 23 pairs.

However, having a larger genome does not necessarily mean having more genes. In this spider, approximately 77% of the genome consists of repetitive DNA sequences that appear many times throughout its genetic material.

The research also highlights an unusual feature of spider chromosomes. Spiders lack the conventional repetitive DNA sequences associated with telomeres, the protective structures at the ends of chromosomes. This difference could help explain why spider chromosomes appear to evolve more rapidly than those of vertebrates.

"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal Tree of Life," Bond said.

Why Is the Spider Named After Stephen Colbert?

The story behind the spider's unusual scientific name dates back to 2008, when Stephen Colbert discovered that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young.

Not wanting to be left out, Colbert turned the situation into a comedy segment. During "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report," he publicly demanded that Bond name a spider in his honor.

Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti became Colbert's namesake in the spider world.

Rising Seas Threaten California's Trapdoor Spiders

Beyond revealing the spider's genetic peculiarities, the research could play an important role in protecting the species.

The genome sequencing effort is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, a state-funded initiative designed to build a collection of genomic information that scientists can use to guide conservation decisions.

Trapdoor spiders generally do not venture far from their burrows, making it difficult for populations to move between habitats. Because their coastal dune environments are already separated into isolated areas, researchers hope genetic information will help them identify distinct populations that may need special protection.

"We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond said. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species."

Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) is found only in coastal dunes along a limited stretch of Central California, extending from the San Francisco Bay area to Monterey.

This restricted range makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental changes. Rising sea levels could eliminate portions of its coastal habitat, while invasive species pose another significant danger.

"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond said.

Spider Venom Could Hold Clues to New Medicines

The potential benefits of studying this spider's genome extend beyond conservation and evolutionary biology. Scientists also hope that understanding spider genetics will help them explore the vast range of chemical compounds found in spider venom.

Some substances identified in spider venoms have shown promise as potential painkillers, while others could be useful in developing new ways to control agricultural pests.

With so many spider species still poorly understood at the genetic level, researchers believe their venoms may contain valuable compounds that have yet to be discovered.

"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," Bond said.

The study's additional authors include Stephen Richards, Emma Jochim, Lacie Newton, James Starrett, Ruta Sahasrabudhe and Oanh Nguyen of UC Davis; Eric Beraut, Colin Fairbairn, Samuel Sacco, William Seligmann and Merly Escalona of UC Santa Cruz; Robert D. Cooper of Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University; and H. Bradley Shaffer and Erin Toffelmier of UCLA.

The research received support from the California Conservation Genomics Project, with funding provided to the University of California through the state of California's State Budget Act of 2019, as well as from the National Science Foundation.

Materials provided by University of California - Davis. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#586. Record Store Day Black Friday’s Most Wanted, 2026: Beatles, Noah Kahan, Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Sombr, Billy Joel, Katseye and Other Vinyl Must-Finds

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic

Record Store Day is back in black. As you likely already know, RSD is a semiannual holiday for vinyl hounds, with the Black Friday edition being a less jam-packed adjunct to the primary event in April — meaning that, this year, for instance, there are “only” 188 titles being released, almost exactly half of the 355 exclusives that were put on sale in the spring event. Even with that lesser amount of limited-edition discs going out onto the shelves, there is truly something for everybody in this list. Or, to put it another way: If you can’t find anything that grabs you in this lineup, then, to quote Leonard Cohen, you don’t really care for music, do ya?

Our best guess is that there will not be utter pandemonium in the indie shops or in the lines outside this Black Friday morning, if only because of the lack of a Taylor, Olivia or Billie title this time. Which does not mean that there will not still be a healthy contingent of young people joining the veteran vinyl geeks in the checkout lines. In an interview published earlier in the week in Variety, RSD co-founder Michael Kurtz said that the majority of customers for Record Store Day events are under 35. That may continue to be the case as this one has titles from hot and/or younger-skewing artists or franchises including Noah Kahan, Katseye, Sombr and the “Wicked” and “Kpop Demon Hunters” films.

That said, boomers are still gonna boom, and they, Gen-X-ers, millennials and others who have a taste for classic rock, soul and jazz — meaning every generation, really — will find something to salivate over in a list of vintage material that includes Bruce Springsteen, Prince, Joni Mitchell, Miles Davis, Billy Joel, Bill Withers, Art Blakey and even a collectible from the Beatles that was added to the list after it was first announced in October.

If you want to see the entire list of 188 vinyl releases (a few of which are also having CD editions made available for the occasion) scroll all the way down. But first, if you will, look at our annotated list of 27 of the titles that we consider most covetable, ranging from Carly Rae Jepsen and Cher EPs to a 10,000 Maniacs boxed set to an expanded version of NRBQ’s classic Christmas album.

14,500 copies on 4x LP; 3,700 copies on 2x CD; black vinyl

Springsteen buffs will not always agree on favorite individual shows from his and the band’s 50-year-plus history, but it’s hard to imagine a single fan not considering the “Born to Run” era to be peak form. or not taking a serious interest in this rendering of a long and loose New Year’s Eve concert at the close of 1975. The only question might be which physical format you want it in, since Sony is offering it for Record Store Day Black Friday in both LP and CD form. The much greater amount of vinyl pressed indicates an obvious consumer preference for vinyl nowadays, but with a concert this length, some may reconsider whether they want to flip sides seven times to get it all and opt for compact disc. Whether you pick up a vinyl slipcase or CD jewel box, there are succinct but sweet liner notes from Erik Flannigan, who points out that, yes, that is the band (except for Bruce) decked out in tuxedos in the photographs in the packaging. Good thing any formality about this wonderful show ends there.

10,000 copies of vinyl 12-inch EP; Alpenglow-colored vinyl

Kahan’s exclusive releases have been among the biggest draws at many recent Record Store Days, which is no surprise, given the ongoing presence of two of his studio albums in the top 10 and stadium tours that sell out instantaneously. Fans will already be familiar with the four songs on this EP — “Lighthouse,” “Staying Still,” A Few of Your Own” and “Orbiter” — since they first appeared as bonus tracks on a digital deluxe edition of his smash “The Great Divide” album (and “Orbiter” is a proper single). But having the four tracks partitioned off into their own separate physical release will be irresistible to diehard stickheads.

It’s not like you’re going to get any songs here that you didn’t already get on the recent “Rubber Soul” 60th anniversary super-deluxe edition… or, for that matter, that you haven’t had access to since 1966. But then, that’s the point: This single LP is a recreation of the exact album that U.S. Beatles fans got in ’66, down to the original stereo mix. But that’s been out of print for a long time… and has never been uin print as a gold-colored record, which is the main novelty here. The good news for Beatles collectors is that it’s been pressed in numbers that fall at the very top end of pressings for Record Store Day; the bad news is that 15,000 still won’t last long.

9,400 copies on 3x vinyl; 2,700 copies on 2x CD; vinyl color is crystal blue curaçao

The Prince estate is really making the most out of the fact that it had a pro-shot film of Prince’s six-month 2006-7 residency in Las Vegas in the can. A film of “3121 Las Vegas Live” will briefly hit the big screen in early December, followed by a Blu-Ray edition for home consumption. In the meantime, if you want a physical manifestation of just the music, Record Store Day participant shops are the place to go. The performance captured here starts at a slow simmer but quickly heats up. Suffice it to say that, after hearing this purely audio version, I’ll be lined up for the movie.

Every time there is a new CD boxed set in the ongoing series of Joni Mitchell archival anthologies, a single live performance from that collection gets broken out to have its own separate LP edition for Record Store Day. No complaints at all about that. This ’72 concert is all Joni, accompanying herself on guitar, piano or dulcimer, all the way to a closing “Circle Game” that does have her suddenly surrounded by a chorus of famous and unfamous friends. Some will prefer Mitchell in her purest early-ish form here, and some may prefer the big band era that followed. But hearing the purity of that voice with an emphasis on the then-recent “Blue” and then-forthcoming “For the Roses” is a knockout experience. The only thing more you could wish for is a gatefold jacket instead of putting both discs in a single sleeve (the product description promises gatefold, but it’s not), or liner notes, but it’s still a handsome-looking as well as -sounding package.

The last Billy Joel live album, released for Record Store Day Black Friday 2025, was “Live From Long Island,” pressed in a quantity of 1,500 copies — and fans are still pissed about that. (Resale copy prices are not completely exorbitant, but they do go for more than $100.) Fortunately, the record company got the message and is putting three times that many of this followup on sale, 4,600, although that still may not completely sate the market for live Joel. It’s a spirited set, from a hyperactive “Angry Young Man” opening forward, recorded Dec. 5, 1976 at Connecticut College for a TV special. It includes 15 never-before-released tracks from either the original live shows or a followup that was done to get better takes for the special. The blurb on the back cover promises that four more tracks will be included in a “Turnstiles” 50th anniversary boxed set coming out next year. But few Joel fans will complain about that wait given the wealth of heretofore unreleased music here.

Boone: 5,000 copies on black and white galaxy vinyl

The Sombr and Benson Boone releases are very similar, in that each is a first-time vinyl issue of the EP that started their major-label careers before they broke a lot bigger with a full album that followed. Bot EPs are also mellower than some of the hit music that followed for these artists — Sombr lives up to his name more here. His EP, at four tracks, is less expansive than Boones, which runs to eight songs, and comes with a 12-by-24 insert that has a poster image on one side and lyrics on the other. Apart from their musical merits, both discs just look fab, pulled out of their sleeves and placed into the wild.

Withers: 2,600 copies on LP; 1,300 copies on CD; LP is black vinyl

Various artists/Sweet Relief: 1,200 copies

Now here’s an unofficial two-fer anyone should think about picking up and turning into a double feature, even if their simultaneous release, coming from different labels, may be coincidental. First, there’s Withers’ own 1974 performance, captured for British TV. You can tell the audio is unedited: Withers is heard telling the studio audience that some of his band members are out sick, and in one case restarting a speech. The relaxed feel carries over to the superlative songs. Meanwhile, I have to give an even more enthusiastic endorsement to a double-LP tribute album put together as a benefit for the Sweet Relief Foundation that includes all-new tracks. I was hoping the great Chris Pierce — one of the closest things we have to a modern-day Withers right now — would be one of the artists chosen, and to my sweet relief, he was, contributing “Better Off Dead.” There are also choice cuts from Rickie Lee Jones, Lady Blackbird, Marilyn McCoo and Billy Davis Jr., Ben Harper and others who know how to mix their own spin on things with takes that feel faithful to Withers’ vibe.

2,600.copies of six-LP boxed set; multiple vinyl colors

Rhino has gotten in the habit of issuing one complete boxed set per RSD event for a renowned artist from the Warner-Elektra catalog of riches, from John Prine to Devo. This one for 10,000 Maniacs, composed of all the albums the group put out before Natalie Merchant split to go solo in 1993, is being seen by fans as a very necessary corrective to the fact that a lot of that stuff has been out of print on vinyl forever. Four studio albums are joined by the pre-fame compendium “Hope Chest” and a newly assembled rarities disc full of delectable covers. Merchant is credited with helping oversee the package, including the design of the physical elements, although the liner notes (which are very good) do not include interviews with her or any of the bandmates who continue to carry on without her. It’s worth noting that all of the albums included except the rarities LP are due to be issued individually early next year, if it’s just one or two you need to pick up. But as a fan from their earliest major-label days, I couldn’t imagine not getting the whole thing right now. A matter of curiosity: All of the box and LP packaging here changes the band’s name to Ten Thousand Maniacs from 10,000 Maniacs (although the numerical usage pops up in the liner notes). Some elements of the album cover art have been changed, along with the band-name logos — it has to be a Merchant thing. But if you pick up the individual issues in a few months, apparently the name and artwork will be as we remember them. (The fact that the albums in this box have different covers is further cemented by the lack of barcodes.) Those peculiarities aside, t’s a great trip down maniacal memory lane.

Jepsen has been nothing but prolific in this era, first issuing “Day and Night” as a hefty double-album, then adding eight additional tracks onto the original 24 for a deluxe edition, “Day and Night (Continued).” that runs to an hour and 55 minutes of material. Some things may be more easily digested in smaller chunks, of course, and this EP — also titled “Day and Night (Continued)” — breaks out those eight fresher tracks and gives them their first appearance in a physical format. Plus, you get still more from her photo shoot at Eagle Rock’s Casa Bianca, the best pizza joint in L.A., and if that’s not reason enough to pick it up, you’ve got eight more.

The previous RSD exclusive editions of the “Wicked” and “Wicked: For Good” sold out so quickly, I never did actually catch a glimpse of either of them in my many store visits. That will probably prove true for this combined set that packages both soundtracks together in a 4-LP set in a slipcase with a poster. (The track list, if accurate as rendered online, leaves out the bonus track that was added onto the original RSD “Wicked” issue.) Good luck hunting this down, unless it turns out every franchise fan was sated by the previous two releases after all, which isn’t likely. It’s gonna be popular.

The first of several releases we’ll mention here produced by “jazz detective” Zefv Feldman is a welcome incursion into the wonderful world of Blakey. It comtbines two previously unreleased performances in Paris, the first from 1963 and sporting famous players like Freddie Hubbard and Wayne Shorter, the second with a different ensemble in ’68. “Moons” were on the band leader’s mind, as the collection includes the two big musical moon shots of the era, “Blue Moon” and “Moon River.” The latter opens the collection and might give Henry Mancini a heart attack if he were still around to have one — it’s like “Moon River” on amphetamines (not speaking literally, friends, just figuratively), and it’s quite a fantastic flood. The liner notes booklet is copious as with almost any Feldman-related release, and even though a CD edition will follow for the general market in a week, it’s always worth picking up the limited-edition vinyl versions of these releases just for the larger type and photographs. And, sure, the wide-open grooves, too.

5,000 copies of 2x LP; on “Third Pyramid Pink” vinyl

I would have taken an interest in a B-52s live set anyway, but this one turns out to be particularly a wowser because of the addition of a three-man horn section that really helps some of the songs rock in an augmented way. Fans may already know this Roseland Ballroom NYC ’82 performance from when it was included in the “Ancient Culture: Mesopotamia Revisited” set, but for those of us who didn’t have that, or anyone who did but just likes a good breakout, it’s a delightful revelation of the band at its early ’80s peak.

3,500 copies of 12-inch vinyl EP; red vinyl

Cher had not released any original material in many years until she came back with a Christmas project that included some songs newly written to add to the holiday tuneage canon. With this EP spinoff, the emphasis is on the dance-ier chestnuts, including three different mixes of “DJ Play a Christmas Song” and an added duet with Kelly Clarkson. The lady-in-red cover shot is different from any previous artwork in her Christmas-music campaign, too.

We were not able to preview this particular release, so we cannot vouch for what the “dance break” versions of three of Katseye’s most popular songs sound like — “Debut,” “Gnarly” and “Gabriela.” But we can tell you the way it will fly off the shelves will be gnarly indeed. All three mixes are congregated on one side of the vinyl, with a mystery etching on the other. Each copy is said to includes two out of six “randomly selected unique photocards,” so fans will be figuring out how to get around the one-copy-per-customer rule in most stores, as if this needed an incentive to sell out faster.

Another archival production from Zev Feldman, who is stretching out from being seen as “just” a jazz guy with his Bobby Womack and Marianne Faithful releases this Record Store Day. Womack can also stretch out, as it turns out, with two numbers in this live set that go past the 12-minute mark, “You’re Welcome, Stop on By” and “Communication” are both over 12 minutes long. Recorded in Paris in 1976, where the liner notes say he was having a higher profile at the time than in the U.S., this collection feels essential as a revelation of just what an expansive showman he was as well as crafter of classic soul singles.

10,000 copies; “Derpy Sussie Splatter” vinyl

The hunt for “Kpop Demon Hunters” collectibles never stops. Record Store Day just had dual editions of the soundtrack that were quick and easy sellouts, but that could hardly stand in the way of yet another version — and surely not the last — this one featuring fresh art created by official “Demon Hunters” production designer Mingjue Helen Chen and visual development artist Marion Bordeyne. We’ll let the product description do the rest of the talking: “This Derpy Sussie Splatter vinyl includes exclusive holographic art on both the front cover and triple gatefold, 3 of 6 mini inserts, 1 of 3 holographic mini inserts, a sticker sheet, and an oversized poster.” You might have to take their word for it since it won’t be surprising if most or all of the copies are gone by the time you get your lazy post-Thanksgiving butt to the shop.

Sax man Getz is the only one with his name above the title on this release, but for the first three of its six sides, legendary guitarist João Gilberto is his equal costar. Together, they recreate the magic they’d made together in a historic studio teaming in one of the few live shows they did together to follow that. All the music here was previously released by Resonance more than a decade ago, but this three-LP set for the first time combines two albums — one of Getz with Gilberto in SF, one without — into an exemplary single package (and the Getz-only half of the equation never made it onto vinyl before). The multiple interviews or essays in the copious liner notes even include a sizable explanation of the bossa nova craze that finds a kind of quiet culmination here.

Fountains of Wayne’s final album before their breakup sometimes gets undervalued because it’s their least comical, most sober outing, perhaps reflecting the more dominant influence of Chris Collingwood, versus the wryer touch favored by Adam Schlesinger, who’d run the show more on the preceding record. Regardless, there’s wit enough here, along with some of the band’s starker songs. It’s been challenging for FoW fans to complete their vinyl collections, since this fast went out of print after a single pressing in 2001. Even now, 2,000 is not a lot, but it’ll be at least enough to satisfy some of us who never stopped believing that this brilliant group had it going on.

This is the “Bitches Brew”-era Miles who took free jazz into the land of psychedelia, if you hadn’t already guessed that from the cover art by his favorite cover painter in the ’60s, Mati Klarwein. It might as well have been recorded at the Fillmore, even though Davis actually had his all-star quintet (Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Dave Holland and Jack DeJohnette) in Copenhagen for a TV taping. The music has previously been heard on a DVD and on a one-time vinyl pressing of just a few hundred copies, but this mastering is said to be a revelation even for the relatively small number of cultists who’ve already heard this dynamic performance in some form.

3,500 copies; on “Pawn Shop Patina”-colored vinyl

As the title and cover hint, this is a collection of cover songs these Dolls have done over the years, and what great taste they’ve had in other bands, as evidenced in a collection that runs from the Plimsouls’ “A Million Miles Away” to the Kinks’ “Catch Me Now, I’m Falling,” with stops for Tom Petty, INXS, Prince and… Supertramp! (A CD and digital release will follow a week after this vinyl exclusive.)

5,000 copies; 3D zoetrope picture-disc vinyl

We did not get a review copy of this, but we’re going to guess from the product description alone that it might be fun, with or without actually listening to what’s in the grooves, just from looking at them. “Zoetrope” discs have been a thing for a while, turning vinyl into animation, but this is the first one we can recall seeing that is billed as a 3D zoetrope disc, with cardboard glasses to put on to enjoy the effect. We look forward to hearing whether the effect of watching that is as mind-bending as the Gizzard boys’ music typically is, and what substances it is best combined with.

1,800 copies on three-sided 2x LP set; black vinyl

We’re still morning Faithful’s passing, so it’s moving to hear her in her prime, or one of her primes, in a performance captured in 1983, after a comeback run of three acclaimed albums on Island, including of course “Broken English.” The tape of the D.C. set ends with the title track from that latter album and is missing a few final songs from the actual performance, so it’s spread across three sides and the fourth is devoted to an etching of a William Blake quote in concentric-circle script.

2,215 copies of six-45-rpm-singles boxed set; different marbled color variations

Jazz Dispensary dispenses something worth picking up for every single RSD edition, and this time they’ve eschewed the usual single-LP compilation format to put out a box of singles. It comes in a candy-style box, with six different vintage singles in different but equally delicious-looking colors, plus some glow-in-the-dark 45 adapters as a bonus. As usual, even though the description calls these “jazz,” the music therein leans more toward the funk side of the fence, from Eddie Jefferson’s honestly groovy “Psychedelic Sally” to Patrice Rushen’s kinda-weird “Kickin’ Back.” Obscure but charming singles from Rusty Bryant, Idris Muhammad, Pleasure and Johnny Hammond are also represented. Will you play these a lot, or easily find shelf space for an odd-shaped package? Probably no in both cases, yet it’s kind of irresistible as a hep novelty package nonetheless.

What could be better for celebrating the season than NRBQ’s 1978 “Merry Christmas From NRBQ” EP? Very possibly, a modern expansion of that project that extends it to 19 tracks, 10 of them making their vinyl debut, one (the closing “Auld Lang Syne”) getting its premiere altogether. We weren’t able to preview this package to tell you whether they do or don’t rock out the newly added “Jesus Loves Me” and “The Christmas Song,” but we hope to score a copy and fill in that part of the NRB-FAQ.

For your printout needs, here’s the full list of 2026 Record Store Day Black Friday exclusives, as released in October:

#585. Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. For approximately one hour, the star gradually grew brighter before fading back to its usual appearance. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no sudden explosion or flare. It looked as though an invisible object had moved between Earth and the star, bending its light in our direction. Afterward, the star returned to normal and showed no further changes in brightness.

Researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown. The event appears to be an example of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. When a compact object with sufficient mass passes in front of a distant star, its gravity bends the star's light and temporarily magnifies its brightness. This produces a recognizable pattern that differs from the changes caused by variable stars, stellar flares, or passing asteroids.

Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team that they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event. What remained uncertain was the nature of the invisible object responsible.

Three Possible Explanations for the Mysterious Object

Researchers have identified three potential explanations for Phoebe. One possibility is a rogue planet that was expelled from its original solar system and now travels alone through the Milky Way. Another is a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud. If the second explanation proves correct, Phoebe would become the first planet discovered through gravitational microlensing beyond our galaxy.

The third possibility is far more extraordinary. Phoebe could be a primordial black hole, an ancient object that formed in the earliest moments of the universe. Unlike ordinary black holes, which develop when massive stars collapse, primordial black holes could have emerged from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang. Such objects would have formed long before the first stars appeared.

A One-Hour Signal Reveals a Surprising Clue

The unusually short duration of the brightening provides an important clue about Phoebe's mass. Gravitational microlensing events depend partly on how massive the intervening object is. Generally, lighter objects produce shorter events, although their speed and position also influence how long the magnification lasts.

Phoebe's signal lasted approximately 60 minutes, placing it near the detection limit of current astronomical surveys. Using the observed duration and their models of the event, researchers estimated that the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon. That would make it considerably less massive than any planet in our solar system and far too small to be a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star.

Black holes produced through stellar collapse typically have masses of at least about five times that of the Sun. Phoebe's estimated mass falls enormously below that threshold. If the mysterious object really is a black hole, its tiny mass would point toward a primordial origin rather than the death of a star.

Could Phoebe Be a Primordial Black Hole Linked to Dark Matter?

To investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations. These included stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo.

The results strongly favored the dark matter halo. According to the team's calculations, Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. This enormous difference makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing, although it does not establish that Phoebe is a primordial black hole.

If the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected. It may have formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Big Bang.

For roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space, leaving almost no trace of its existence. Then, on a single night in December 2019, its gravity may have briefly magnified the light of a distant star, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe.

#583. The Killers Guitarist Dave Keuning Survived ‘Major Stroke’ With ‘40% Chance of Survival’: ‘I Can Play Guitar Just as Good as Before’

Dave Keuning, guitarist for The Killers, said that he survived a “major stroke” two weeks ago that had a “40% chance of survival” but he’s still able to “play guitar just as good as before.” He revealed the news on Thanksgiving, along with announcing the birth of his daughter.

“Happy Thanksgiving, everyone! Three months ago, we had our baby girl, Odette,” Keuning wrote. “Two weeks ago, I had a major stroke, and thanks to my wife acting fast, I went straight to the hospital and into surgery. The first hour after a stroke is critical when it comes to getting to the hospital. I had a blood clot in my brain that cut off the blood supply to the entire right side of my brain. By the time I arrived at the hospital, I was blind in one eye and had lost function on my left side, but I still wasn’t able to realize I was having a stroke. The doctors said I had a 40% chance of survival and I would have disabilities after, but by some miracle I am fine.” Related Stories The Best Audible Books to Listen to Right Now: 'ACOTAR,' 'Hunger Games,' 'Pride & Prejudice' and More John Travolta Didn’t Recognize Himself as Alleged JFK Assassin Johnny Roselli in ‘November 1963’: ‘I Went, "Oh My God, He’s the Devil"’

Keuning thanked his Killers bandmates, including lead singer Brandon Flowers, drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr. and bassist Mark Stoermer, for their support during his recovery.

“And yes I can play guitar just as good as before,” Keuning wrote. “It was the first thing I checked when I woke up from surgery. I feel extremely fortunate that I am alive and well, and that I can use my hands and feet and talk just like before. I am thankful for my wife, my son, my daughter, and all of my bandmates, who I feel closer to than ever.”

I've been Black Friday bargain hunting for a long time and I'm here to tell you how to avoid getting scammed. From fraudulent sites to fake goods, my guide will help you shop safely online.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There are some real bargains to be had this Black Friday, including discounts on telescopes, cameras, drones, Lego and streaming to watch your favorite sci-fi. Heck, we're even offering the chance to win a smart telescope worth $419!

But as exciting as all the Black Friday deals are, there's the very real risk that you could get scammed, particularly given how exciting it is to snag a deal.

That's where my scam-spotting guide comes in. Not only do I get paid to hunt down Black Friday savings, but I've also snapped up more stargazing deals than I care to think about, and I know how to spot a shady offer or suspect site. So, read on and I'll show you how to stay safe online this Black Friday.

The best way to avoid getting scammed is to take advantage of our carefully curated Black Friday Deals. We put the work in to find you the best deals on stargazing equipment, cameras, tech and even toys, double and triple-checking that they're genuine savings from reputable retailers.

And if you're hunting for deals on your own, you should do the same; shop with known and trusted retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy, Target and others. Ideally, you'll want items that are sold and shipped by that retailer; you can usually tell if that's the case by looking at the buy box, the area with 'Buy Now', 'Add to Cart ', or similar.

Some sites, Amazon included, let third-party companies sell through their sites. That's not a scam, and most are legitimate. However, I'd still recommend you check out the seller's feedback and if you see a lot of negative feedback, you should probably steer clear.

In doubt? Myself and a team of experts spend all of Black Friday finding the best, most reliable deals from reputable retailers so you don't have to, testing links and checking they're legitimate and safe. We'll drop our favorites into the page below, but check out our Black Friday Deals page for more.

Disney Plus is the home of both the Star Wars and Marvel cinematic universes. You can save 62% by getting the Disney and Hulu ad-supported bundle and get two huge libraries of content for less than $5 a month.

Save 77% by signing up for two years of NordVPN's Prime plan (nothing to do with Amazon) and getting three months extra for free. There are also other cheaper options which offer lesser savings.

NordVPN features an ad and tracker blocker, anti-malware protection, a data breach scanner, browsing protection and much more.

However, while Amazon, Best Buy and so on have been around for a long time, it's surprisingly easy to set up a fake website. Here's how to check if a website is secure.

Even if the website isn't an imitation, it's important to be wary of sites that pop up offering massive discounts. While lightning deals are absolutely a thing, some of these sites offer fake countdowns in an effort to pressure you into buying goods. If you see one of the best smart telescopes for a quarter of its normal price, for example, you should immediately be suspicious.

Your credit card or debit card may offer some protection if you are scammed but you should always be wary. Other warnings include misspelled product names, stock text, buttons that don't work and other oddities. You can also use a domain name checker to find out how old a website is. If the website was registered just a few months ago, that's a big red flag.

Save $200 on what we've ranked as one of the best telescopes on the market today. You can see everything from nearby planets to far-reaching deep sky objects with bright and sharp views across the entire frame.

Save on a telescope that has featured in our best telescopes guide since our hands-on Celestron NexStar 4SE review early in 2023.

If you're shopping for a Black Friday bargain for the space or sci-fi fan in your life, it's important to keep an eye out for off-brand and fake goods. Not all building block sets are Lego, for example, and there's nothing illegal about other companies making their own sets, but it could lead to disappointment come Christmas Day. And there are also shady companies who will sell direct copies of existing Lego sets. We have a guide to imitation Lego, but the shortcut is to just look out for the Lego logo.

You may come across unfamiliar brands of telescopes, binoculars and other gear. Often, companies will take a generic product, add their own branding, and sell it at a markup. There's no guarantee that product will last and support may well be lacking. Reading a product's feedback can help, but I've also stumbled across many suspicious reviews.

Then there are some products that are just copies of branded goods; forgeries, essentially. I've seen knock-off MicroSD cards, bootleg chargers, and even Celestron has had to warn against fraudulent websites and fake telescopes. The best advice in this regard is to use trusted websites and remember that if a deal is too good to be true, it probably isn't.

Save on one of the best star projectors. In our Pococo Galaxy Projector review, we loved how vibrant and bright the projections appear and that there is a heap of add-on disks available.

Even if you've grabbed a great Black Friday deal, you still need to take steps to protect your identity. One of the best ways to do that is with one of the best VPN services and, this Black Friday there are huge savings on NordVPN and Surfshark. Both services shield you from hackers, hiding your true location and, depending on the tier you choose, can alert you if your identity is compromised. Plus, if you're away from home this holiday season, they're handy for accessing the best sci-fi streaming services.

Save big on Paramount's Premium Plan for two months. Paramount Plus is the home of all Star Trek content as well as its considerable library of original content.

Hackers aside, phishing scams are another risk to your online safety and security. If you get an email that claims to be from a retailer, there's the possibility it's a phishing scam, looking to steal your details. Here are some warning signs:

A common phishing scam I've seen, and one which I almost fell for, is fake emails from a shipping company, telling you there's an extra charge on a package. Click through and the scammer will steal your money and/or credit card details. The best option, if you genuinely have ordered something, is to go to the official website you ordered from and click on your order history. And above all, never, ever share your passwords with anyone, friend or otherwise.

#581. Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret

Carbon is essential to every living thing on Earth, from microscopic organisms to humans. Yet scientists are still working to answer a fundamental question about our planet's history: Where did all this carbon originally come from?

A new study of volcanic rocks from Hawaii offers a surprising possible answer. Researchers have uncovered chemical evidence suggesting that much of Earth's carbon may have arrived aboard ancient meteorites during a particular stage of the planet's formation. Even more remarkably, the findings suggest that some of this carbon became trapped deep inside Earth's core before eventually making its way back to the surface.

The discovery centers on unusual carbon dioxide signatures preserved in volcanic rocks. Researchers believe these chemical fingerprints may reveal carbon that originated in Earth's core and traveled upward through the planet's interior.

"We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth's core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface," says lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor in Columbia University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How Carbon Could Escape From Earth's Core

To understand how carbon might travel from Earth's deepest interior to its surface, it helps to look at the planet's internal structure.

Beneath Earth's thin outer crust lies the mantle, a vast region of mostly solid rock extending approximately 1,800 miles downward. Below that is the outer core, a roughly 1,400-mile-thick layer of molten metal surrounding the extremely hot, dense, solid metallic inner core.

Scientists believe that most of Earth's carbon is stored in its core. However, directly examining this material is far beyond the reach of current technology, and researchers may never be able to obtain samples from such extreme depths.

Fortunately, Earth's volcanic activity offers another way to investigate what lies below.

Recent studies suggest that certain elements can escape from the outer core and enter the overlying mantle. From there, they may be transported toward the surface by enormous rising columns of hot rock known as mantle plumes.

These plumes begin near the boundary between the core and mantle. As they ascend, some of the rock partially melts, producing magma that can eventually erupt through volcanoes.

When that magma cools, crystals begin to grow. Occasionally, these crystals trap tiny droplets of molten material before dissolved gases have a chance to escape. The trapped droplets, known as undegassed melt inclusions, preserve valuable chemical information about the original magma.

"These melts are fossils of the magma," Moussallam says.

Because magma contains dissolved gases, including carbon dioxide, these microscopic pockets provide scientists with a rare opportunity to study carbon that may have traveled upward from Earth's core.

Hawaiian Volcanoes Reveal an Unusual Carbon Signature

Hawaii is particularly well suited for this kind of investigation. Previous research has established that its volcanoes receive magma associated with a deep mantle plume, potentially providing access to material originating near the boundary with Earth's core.

Moussallam and his colleagues examined volcanic rocks from eruptions at Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift. Using a recently developed analytical technique, they measured carbon isotopes preserved inside undegassed melt inclusions.

Carbon isotopes are different forms of the same element that have slightly different masses. By comparing their relative abundance, scientists can identify chemical signatures that offer clues about where carbon came from and what processes it experienced.

The Tantalus Rift samples are thought to represent magma originating near the outer margins of the mantle plume. Earlier research established that typical mantle carbon has an isotopic signature between approximately -5 and -7 per mil, a measurement expressing small differences in isotope ratios. The researchers found that the Tantalus Rift samples closely matched this expected range.

The Kīlauea samples, however, told a very different story.

Magma beneath Kīlauea is believed to originate closer to the center of the mantle plume, where material may rise from near the core-mantle boundary. In these samples, the scientists detected carbon with a much heavier isotopic signature of approximately -1 per mil.

This unusual value has rarely been observed before and differs substantially from the signature normally associated with Earth's mantle.

"This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle," says Moussallam. "This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core."

Although the team considers Earth's core the most likely source, Moussallam emphasizes that the evidence is not yet definitive. Additional measurements will be necessary to establish whether the carbon truly originated there.

Ancient Meteorites May Explain Where Earth's Carbon Came From

The unusual carbon signature also provided researchers with a possible clue about events that occurred more than 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was still forming.

According to Moussallam, the isotopic composition of carbon in Earth's core should preserve "the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created."

To investigate that possibility, the team compared the distinctive Kīlauea measurements with carbon signatures found in ancient meteorites. They discovered similarities to a group of meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites.

Chondrites are among the oldest known materials in our solar system, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. They preserve clues about the primitive material from which planets formed.

"All of Earth is made of chondrites," Moussallam explains. "They're the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets."

Scientists generally distinguish between two broad categories of chondrites. Noncarbonaceous chondrites formed in the inner solar system, while carbonaceous chondrites, which contain more carbon, originated in the outer regions of the solar system.

Exactly how much each type contributed to Earth's formation has remained a subject of scientific debate.

The new findings support the possibility that carbonaceous chondrites made an especially important contribution during the later stages of Earth's development.

According to the researchers' proposed explanation, these carbon-rich meteorites struck the growing planet at a time when it had become better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have accumulated deep within Earth, eventually becoming part of the planet's enormous internal carbon reservoir.

Over billions of years, carbon from that reservoir could have migrated upward through mantle plumes and emerged in volcanic eruptions.

If the interpretation is correct, some of the carbon essential to life today may have arrived from the outer solar system aboard meteorites during Earth's earliest history.

A Remarkable Journey From Space to Life on Earth

Despite the intriguing evidence, important questions remain unanswered. The researchers have not conclusively demonstrated that the unusual carbon came from Earth's core or established precisely how much of the planet's carbon was delivered by carbonaceous meteorites.

"We don't really know. We need more measurements," cautions Moussallam.

Nevertheless, the findings offer a fascinating possible connection between the formation of the solar system, the inaccessible depths of our planet, and the carbon that makes life possible.

They also raise the possibility that some of the carbon found in living organisms today has followed an extraordinary path. After arriving on Earth billions of years ago, it may have become incorporated into the planet's metallic core, moved slowly upward through the mantle, and eventually returned to the surface through volcanic eruptions.

"It's fun to think about. We're made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet's core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting."

The study was coauthored by Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, and Bridgett Holman of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory; Damanveer S. Grewal of Yale University; Estelle F. Rose-Koga of Institut des Sciences de la Terre d'Orléans; Allan Lerner of the US Geological Survey; Paul J. Wallace of the University of Oregon; and Natália Gauer.

Materials provided by Columbia Climate School. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#579. ‘Summer Meadow’ Directors Confront ‘Hypocrisy’ in Films About Migrants: ‘It’s as Though Black and Arab People Are Forbidden to Dream’

The seemingly unremarkable movement of flocks of sheep across the French Alps took on a deeper significance for filmmakers Naël Khleifi and Lisa Debauche. The animals could freely cross borders that certain human beings could not.

That observation was among the starting points for “Summer Meadow,” which explores migration, the complexities of exile and the universal desire to discover the world against a backdrop of the quiet rhythms of pastoral life. Related Stories India Targets at Least 10 Million AI Workers Through National AI Talent Mission, WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Hears Record Store Day Co-Founder on How Black Friday Evolved Into a Major Holiday for Vinyl Hounds, and What Will Fly Off the Shelves This Year

“There are shepherds in Lebanon, in Palestine, in France. They’re everywhere,” Debauche says. “There’s something in that timelessness that allowed us to question contemporary issues without confining the film to current events.”

Following an award-winning run at Locarno and the Cairo Film Festival, the Belgian-French feature screened at the Doha Film Festival in the Ajyal Feature Film Competition, judged by a youth jury. The film follows Hana (Manal Issa), a young Lebanese apprentice shepherdess who seeks refuge in the French Alps. Her encounters with fellow shepherdess Lisa (Sibylle Bataille) and a Moroccan migrant, Kebir (Elkebir Belfatmi), gradually draw her out of her isolation.

For Khleifi, a Belgian-Palestinian filmmaker whose 2021 documentary “Alpes” followed residents and activists secretly helping migrants cross the French-Italian border by night, pastoral life offered another means of exploring migration, freedom and the exploitation of humans and nature.

In challenging conventional narratives of migration, Khleifi identified with Kebir’s journey, driven as much by curiosity and a desire to discover the world as by a search for economic opportunities. “It’s something I know from within,” he tells Variety. “My father’s desire to leave Palestine came from a place that pushed him to leave for many reasons, but also from a desire to discover the world.”

Khleifi contrasts the portrayal of European immigrants in Western cinema with that of Black and Arab migrants. “It’s as though Black and Arab people are forbidden to dream. It drives me crazy,” he says, exasperated. “At some point, we have to turn the question back on the West and confront its hypocrisy. This film is a cry. We’re human beings too. Everyone has the right to dream.”

“Each story is different and rich, each journey, each feeling experienced, each past,” adds first-time director Debauche. “We so often put people into categories. We shut them in boxes, and with this film we wanted to break those boxes open.”

The filmmakers also sought to blur the boundaries between documentary and fiction. “In ‘Alpes,’ I tried to break away from the conventions of documentary filmmaking, particularly the way migration is so often depicted,” Khleifi explains. “Here, I thought to myself, ‘We’re going to make a fiction film using the techniques of documentary.’ It’s a continuation of my cinematic exploration.”

Though meticulously written, the screenplay continued to evolve throughout production. During 10 days of preparation before filming, conversations with Issa helped deepen Hana’s character, while Debauche encouraged first-time actress Bataille to move beyond scripted dialogue and speak in her own words.

Those exchanges, Debauche notes, gave the film an added measure of soul. “We can spend months, years writing, trying to get as close as possible to a character. But reality is always much stronger than fiction.” She goes on, “Our conversations brought us so much, shifted something in us, too, and contributed to the depth of the characters and the story.”

The filmmakers also resisted the temptation to explain their characters’ every motivation. “There’s something beautiful about leaving certain things unexplained,” observes Debauche. “It allows viewers to bring their own questions to the film and find their own meaning in the story.”

Hana’s search for refuge, in Khleifi’s view, reflects a broader sense of unease that characterizes modern life. “With the climate crisis, wars, the far right, capitalism and this collective anxiety, we’re all a little messed up,” he says. “Everyone is trying to find a place where they can come up for air.”

Before joining the project, Issa had grown disillusioned with the film industry’s response to the war in Gaza and began questioning whether she wanted to continue making films.

“In films, we’re always talking about human beings. All of a sudden, children are dying in atrocious ways and we don’t want to talk about it anymore,” Issa laments. “I found myself asking why I was doing this. Had I spent years of my life doing a job where you’re afraid to say, ‘Stop killing children’?”

“Summer Meadow” gave Issa both the freedom to express herself and an opportunity to rethink her craft. Working alongside nonprofessional actors and the flocks of sheep allowed her to relinquish control, an experience she likens to an acting workshop, adding that she would carry those lessons into future projects.

“With the sheep, you can’t say, ‘Now I’m going to position myself like this,’” she explains. “I wanted to be out of control. For me, acting is being.”

Having left Lebanon for France at 13, Issa found herself reconsidering her own relationship with freedom through conversations with Belfatmi about his experience of migration. “For me, I had been torn away from my country. All I wanted was to come back,” she recalls. “But had I really experienced life?”

As Khleifi and Debauche edited the film in Europe, Issa was in Beirut amid the Israeli bombardment of the Lebanese capital, a reality that informed their decision to close the film with images of Lebanon.

The friendship between Hana and Lisa, Debauche believes, speaks to the importance of being genuinely available to others. “I think it’s through our encounters with others that we perhaps come closer to ourselves,” she reflects. “These two women have very different stories. At first glance, apart from the sheep and their work, what could they possibly share? And yet, a sense of trust develops between them that allows them to make peace with certain things.”

Issa experienced that firsthand. Increasingly isolated since the onset of the war, she found solace in her friendship with the filmmakers. Debauche encouraged her to share her experiences, both in conversation and on paper, some of which found their way into the screenplay.

“I lived through the same thing Hana did. That’s what’s beautiful. The film came at the right time in my life. It was as though Lisa Debauche was for me what Lisa in the film was for Hana. It opened me up, made me speak out more.”
